tldr: Instead of relying on reward shaping, this framework has LLM multi-agents generate coarse reference trajectories as code, then turns them into physically executable policies via imitation reinforcement learning (DeepMimic). Tested on a wheeled quadruped robot (Go2-W), it generated diverse skills—from flips to handstand walking—and demonstrated successful Sim-to-Real transfer directly onto the hardware.
hero_caption: Overall flow of MimicAgent. Given a text prompt, LLM agents iteratively refine and generate a coarse reference trajectory (green). Using this as a target in reinforcement learning (DeepMimic), the system learns a physically consistent policy (blue).
overview:
When teaching quadruped robots dynamic, high-level skills like flips or spins via reinforcement learning (RL), the biggest hurdle is reward shaping. Changing a single weight even slightly can lead to unexpected falls or bizarre movements. This has normalized hours of manual trial-and-error by researchers—often dubbed "graduate student descent." Recent attempts like Eureka use LLMs to write reward functions automatically. However, they struggle to generalize across diverse skills and complex robot morphologies, leaving the fundamental issue that humans must still carefully craft task-specific evaluation metrics.

The authors turned this problem on its head. Their core observation: for both humans and LLMs, generating target reference motions directly ("move like this") is far more intuitive and easier than fiddling with reward equations. While humanoid robotics has seen huge success with example-guided RL using large-scale motion capture (MoCap) datasets, quadruped robots lack such reference motion data. So, why not have an LLM create them?

The proposed framework, MimicAgent, is an agentic pipeline that turns text prompts into motion plans, generates forward kinematics code, and outputs reference trajectories while self-correcting physical invalidities using generic unit tests. The generated trajectories are coarse and ignore physics simulations. Yet, feeding them as guides into DeepMimic-based imitation RL elevates them into dynamic control policies that obey physical laws.

In experiments on a wheeled quadruped robot (Unitree Go2-W), MimicAgent successfully produced 65 diverse skills. It yielded smoother trajectories in less time than manual human keyframing, scored significantly higher in prompt-following than Eureka in user studies, and successfully transferred directly to the real robot (Sim-to-Real).
contributions: Proposed the MimicAgent framework, which automatically creates target motion trajectories for quadruped robots from text prompts through a code-generation and self-refinement loop.

Implemented a mechanism that filters and self-corrects reference trajectories using only task-agnostic unit tests (such as base height and joint limits), without needing any task-specific fitness functions.
Demonstrated that even coarse kinematic trajectories ignoring physics can be trained into real-world deployable policies via imitation RL and a Sim-to-Real pipeline.
Empirically showed that prompting in the trajectory space is superior to reward-space search (Eureka) in exploration efficiency, expressiveness, and token consumption.

sections.heading: Escaping the reward trap: Having LLMs sketch trajectories instead of formulas
sections.summary: Reward shaping has long been a bottleneck in acquiring quadruped skills via RL, and automated LLM reward design (like Eureka) struggles across diverse robot morphologies and tasks. Because quadrupeds lack large-scale MoCap data, this work proposes MimicAgent. It uses LLM coding agents to generate coarse reference trajectories directly from text, then distills them into physically valid policies through imitation learning.
sections.details:
In recent years, reinforcement learning (RL) has enabled legged robots to demonstrate remarkable agility and robustness. However, this success relies heavily on meticulously tuned reward functions. For complex and dynamic skills, extensive manual trial-and-error—the notorious "graduate student descent"—has been unavoidable.

To tackle this, recent works like Eureka use LLMs to automate reward design. Yet, these methods require human-designed, task-specific fitness functions to evaluate candidate rewards. They remain brittle when applied to diverse skills and complex morphologies like wheeled quadrupeds, frequently failing to align with the prompt's intent.

Meanwhile, in humanoid robotics, "example-guided RL" has achieved great success by using large-scale motion capture (MoCap) datasets as demonstration references. Quadruped robots, however, lack such rich, diverse motion datasets.

This led the authors to propose MimicAgent. The key insight is that for both humans and LLMs, generating reference motions is far easier than shaping reward functions. The LLM generates executable code specifying the robot's base and foot trajectories, which are converted into kinematically sound trajectories via MuJoCo's forward kinematics (FK). Because these trajectories bypass physical simulation, they are dynamic approximations; ensuring physical consistency is delegated entirely to the subsequent imitation RL (DeepMimic) stage.

captions.F1: The end-to-end pipeline from text prompt to imitation RL. Using coarse reference trajectories (green) generated by LLM agents as demonstrations, an imitation policy (blue) is trained within a physics simulator.

sections.heading: The current state of quadruped locomotion and text-to-control robotics
sections.summary: Quadruped robot control is shifting from classical MPC toward RL-based imitation learning, alongside rapid progress in generating robot behaviors from natural language. However, existing language-conditioned policies require massive paired datasets, and LLM code-generation methods struggle with choosing the right intermediate representation. This study introduces a fresh approach: directly synthesizing reference trajectories with an LLM for imitation learning.
sections.details:
### Evolution of Quadruped Locomotion
Quadruped locomotion has a long history. Classical approaches predominantly used Model Predictive Control (MPC) to track contact patterns for trotting, bounding, and galloping. However, MPC relies on hand-crafted reference trajectories, is computationally heavy, and limits behavioral diversity. Recently, imitation RL has enabled more intuitive and acrobatic behaviors, such as bipedal standing and whole-body manipulation.

### Text-to-Robot Control
Prior work on driving robots from language instructions broadly falls into two categories:
- Language-conditioned end-to-end policies: These map natural language directly to joint commands. However, collecting large-scale paired datasets of text and diverse robotic locomotion is notoriously difficult.
- LLM code and intermediate representation generation: These use LLMs as high-level planners or control-code generators, translating top-level instructions into low-level motor commands.

This work follows the latter line of research but takes a unique angle: instead of generating reward functions, it directly synthesizes reference trajectories that serve as targets for imitation learning.

sections.heading: Multi-agent trajectory synthesis and the Sim-to-Real pipeline
sections.summary: MimicAgent consists of a four-stage agent loop: motion planning, code generation, kinematic execution, and self-correction. Generated motions are validated against task-agnostic unit tests; failures are diagnosed and revised by agent feedback. The resulting trajectories train a privileged Teacher policy via PPO, which is then distilled (DAgger) into a Student policy relying only on real-world onboard observations for deployment.
sections.details:
### Agentic Motion Synthesis Pipeline
MimicAgent uses a multi-agent structure that progressively turns text prompts into concrete motions (Fig. F2):
1. **Motion Planner Agent**: Writes a detailed textual plan outlining the skill's high-level intent, stabilization strategy, sub-phase breakdown over normalized phase $\phi \in [0, 1]$, foot contact states, base linear/angular velocity commands, and foot trajectories.
2. **Code Generator Agent**: Translates the plan into a Python program that outputs base position $\mathbf{p}_t^{\text{base}}$, base orientation (quaternion) $\boldsymbol{\alpha}_t^{\text{base}}$, and joint angles $\boldsymbol{\theta}_t$.
3. **Kinematic Executor**: Executes the Python code in MuJoCo using forward kinematics (FK) to obtain keyframe states $\boldsymbol{\tau} = \{s_0, \dots, s_T\}$ across discrete phases. It runs fast because it skips physical simulation.

### Task-Agnostic Unit Tests and the Self-Correction Loop
Instead of crafting task-specific success criteria like Eureka, MimicAgent evaluates "structural validity" common to all skills:
- **Base Height Range**: Penalized if the base drops below 0.1 m from the ground or exceeds twice its standing height.
- **Joint Limit Violations**: Penalized based on the number of violated joint limits $N_{\text{violated}}$.
- **Floor Penetration**: Evaluates the depth and frequency of feet sinking into the ground.
- **Air-time Constraints**: Requires that non-aerial skills maintain at least one foot on the ground for at least half of the motion cycle.

If tests fail, the **Motion Diagnosis Agent** analyzes the cause in natural language, and the **Code Modification Agent** rewrites the code. This self-refinement loop runs for up to $N=3$ iterations.

### Imitation RL and Sim-to-Real (Teacher-Student Distillation)
Using the coarse trajectories, goal-conditioned RL based on DeepMimic is trained on the Unitree Go2-W (16 DOFs: 12 leg joints and 4 wheels).
- **Teacher Policy**: Observes privileged simulator state $s^{\text{priv}}_t$ (true velocities, link positions, contact flags, global yaw) and is trained via PPO to track the reference trajectory.
- **Student Policy**: Acts on proprioceptive data available from onboard sensors (joint angles, velocities, and a 50-step history $H$) plus a yaw-invariant projected gravity vector $\hat{\mathbf{g}}_t$ to avoid IMU drift.
- **Distillation**: After the Teacher converges, DAgger trains the Student via behavioral cloning ($\lVert a_t - \hat{a}_t \rVert^2$). Domain randomization and observation noise ensure robust Sim-to-Real transfer.

captions.F2: Internal architecture of MimicAgent. A prompt is converted into a motion plan, coded, executed kinematically, and checked via task-agnostic unit tests. On failure, a diagnosis agent provides feedback to automatically refine the code.

sections.heading: Outperforming manual keyframing and baselines in motion quality and hardware tests
sections.summary: In a 57-participant user study, MimicAgent significantly outperformed Eureka in prompt alignment across most skills. It produced smoother trajectories faster than manual keyframing and matched or exceeded expert-tuned RL controllers in gait cycle consistency. The authors also demonstrated novel "skating" maneuvers and real-world deployment on the Go2-W, including bipedal handstand walking.
sections.details:
### Baseline Comparisons and User Study
MimicAgent was evaluated against Eureka and manually created keyframes (via a GUI tool, trained with DeepMimic) across 7 skills—from standard Go2 trotting to Go2-W flips—in a blind 5-point Likert survey with 57 participants.
MimicAgent dramatically outperformed Eureka on most skills, including front flip (+3.5), side flip (+3.5), trot (+1.8), aerial crossover (+2.3), and crab diagonal scuttle (+2.4). Despite being given task-specific fitness functions, Eureka failed to consistently acquire dynamic behaviors on the complex wheeled quadruped.

### Annotation Time and Trajectory Quality
Comparing GUI-based manual keyframing to MimicAgent, the agent completed motions consistently faster. While human authoring time spikes for complex, asymmetric leg coordination, the LLM codes them at a steady pace.
Furthermore, tracking error (MSE) analysis showed that policies trained on MimicAgent trajectories achieved lower errors across all global position, orientation, and velocity metrics than those trained on manual human keyframes. The mathematical function-based trajectories from the LLM were both spatially and temporally smoother than human hand-tuning.

### Comparison with Expert-Designed Policies (Walk-These-Ways)
Using Waveform Morphology Analysis (WMA), MimicAgent was compared to the hand-tuned "Walk-These-Ways" (WTW) controller. For trotting (target 1.0 m/s), MimicAgent achieved 0.9999 m/s—one-sixth the velocity error of WTW—with gait cycle consistency of 0.958 (vs. 0.865 for WTW), exhibiting metronome-like precision. In bounding, it achieved 30% lower velocity error and spontaneously discovered a distinct flight phase with a 39.4% duty factor.

### Computational Cost and Token Consumption
While Eureka evaluates 80 candidate rewards iteratively per skill and consumes massive amounts of tokens, MimicAgent required roughly 1/42nd the token count. GPU training times were comparable (~46 to 51 hours). The authors note that Eureka's bottleneck is not search budget, but its fundamental difficulty in discovering intended behaviors within the reward space.

### Unit Test Ablation and Failure Modes
Ablating unit tests revealed that combining air-time and floor-penetration constraints is vital; removing either leads to degenerate solutions where the robot burrows into the ground.
Analyzing the failed skills (the remaining 8% out of a 92% success rate) showed that all involved prolonged aerial rotations. When an LLM generates an unphysical reference trajectory with floaty, overly slow ascents, the robot cannot follow it physically. The policy falls into a local minimum: standing still while merely wiggling its joints, which still harvests substantial tracking rewards.

captions.F3: Taxonomy of 65 skills automatically proposed and generated by the LLM. They span evenly across Active (wheel-driven), Passive (leg-driven), and Hybrid modalities across 6 categories, showing the method is not biased toward a narrow action space.
captions.F4: Representative skills synthesized in simulation. The system masters novel, advanced behaviors, such as skating by gliding while balancing solely on front legs.
captions.F5: Real-world deployment on the Unitree Go2-W robot. Left: two-legged handstand walk; Right: front-wheel wheelie roll, verifying successful Sim-to-Real transfer.

sections.heading: Takeaway: A new path for robot learning beyond reward engineering
sections.summary: MimicAgent establishes a new paradigm for quadruped imitation learning by having LLM agents synthesize coarse, kinematically valid reference trajectories. Bypassing manual reward shaping and the lack of quadruped MoCap data, it demonstrates that diverse and dynamic skills can be acquired efficiently both in simulation and on real hardware.
sections.details:
This paper presented MimicAgent, a framework that automates quadruped trajectory generation using LLM agents.

By leveraging coding agents to directly synthesize "coarse yet kinematically plausible reference motions," the approach avoids both the fragility of reward engineering and the massive manual effort it requires. It also unlocks imitation learning for quadrupeds, which inherently lack large-scale MoCap datasets like those available for humanoids.

Experiments confirmed that the generated reference trajectories are more than sufficient to learn robust, expressive behaviors, substantially beating Eureka in perceived instruction alignment. Rather than searching through sensitive, abstract reward formulas, collaborating with LLMs to sketch trajectories directly proves to be an exceptionally promising direction for robotic skill acquisition.

takeaways: Generating coarse trajectories is far more intuitive and less prone to failure for both LLMs and humans than generating reward functions.
Even when reference trajectories are physically ungrounded kinematic approximations (FK), downstream imitation RL (DeepMimic) successfully refines them into physics-compliant policies.
Without task-specific fitness functions, generic unit tests (height, joint limits, ground penetration) are sufficient to drive an effective LLM self-correction loop.
A Teacher-Student setup (distilling privileged information with yaw-invariant observations) enables policies trained on LLM trajectories to deploy directly to real hardware without extra fine-tuning.
limitations: If the LLM outputs unrealistic aerial trajectories with floaty air-times, imitation RL can get stuck in a local minimum where the robot stands still and just moves its joints.
Passing unit tests does not guarantee that the motion matches the user's semantic intent; human verification may still be required.
Because current kinematic generation ignores contact forces and friction limits, RL convergence can struggle on behaviors demanding extreme torques or controlled slipping.
